units.translation: I tear apart, an unusual present form, from which the second aorist φλαδεῖν [to tear apart] is derived.
The scholiast explains it by ἐρράγησαν [they burst apart]. See Thes. vol. 8 p. 921.
And the linen-destroying tatters of the garments burst apart under the pains.
which the scholiast explains as ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ λάμπει, κἂν διὰ σκότου χωρῇ [it shines in every place, even if it goes through darkness].
The desire of Zeus blazes everywhere, even in black darkness, with fortune for mortal peoples.
it shines in every place, even if it goes through darkness
Which is more often called Φλέγρας ς. Φλεγραῖον πεδίον [the Phlegraean plain]: see Thes. vol. 8 p. 933. Phlegra was a city of Thrace.
where φλέγουσαν [blazing] refers to φλόγα [flame], which is contained in the words φλογός μέγαν πώγωνα [the great beard of flame].
when the blazing sun with its rays ceases to scorch the earth.
For the bright circle of the sun, blazing with its rays, passed through the middle of the sky.
Zeus hurling the thunderbolt from his hand.
the sky blazing beneath the stars.
And the torch blazes, armed in their hands.
the great beard of flame blazing,
the eye of a young woman blazing will not escape my notice.
before swift-rushing words arrive and blaze under the pressure of need.
Am I a false prophet, a door-knocking babbler?
But you have no strength, nor veins flowing with blood.

Thus Hermann: in M is γεμόντων θυμέλαι φλεγόντων [the altars being full, blazing], with the gloss γεμόντων [being full] inserted, which was written as a note to φλεόντων [abounding] (now corrupted into φλεγόντων [blazing]). Hesychius explains φλεῖ [it abounds] by γέμει, εὐκαρπεῖ, πολυκαρπεῖ [it is full, it bears well, it bears much].
and the altars of the elders, receiving the old (Hermann added προβούλοις [counsellors]), abounding.
it is full, it bears well, it bears much
and the burning heat that destroys the eyes of the plants.
The accusative form is heteroclitic, as if from φλογώψ [fiery-eyed].
crossing the surge of the sea.

Thus I restored from Hesychius (s.v. προσαιθρίζουσα [exposing to the air]) for φρουρὰ πλέον καίουσα τῶν εἰρημένων [a watch burning more than the things mentioned], which is read in M, invented by an interpolator.
roasted by the bright flame of the sun.
the descending thunderbolt breathing out flame.
he will find a flame stronger than the thunderbolt.
let the smoky flame be hurled.
with thunder and the flame of the thunderbolt.
the circle of the sun passed through the middle of the sky, warming with its flame.
a watch exposing to the air the escorting flame.
the heart set on fire by the new commands of the flame.
kindling the flame of the mountain wood.
